stem:
A 66-year-old man with advanced emphysema is seen by the respiratory physiotherapist. He becomes very short of breath climbing the stairs at home. She teaches him to breathe in gently through his nose and then breathe out for twice as long through pursed lips, as if blowing out a candle. He finds that he recovers more quickly afterwards.

How does this breathing pattern help him?

options.A: It raises the breathing rate so that minute ventilation increases
options.B: It lifts arterial carbon dioxide to strengthen the drive to breathe
options.C: It generates a forceful expiration that helps clear sputum
options.D: It warms and humidifies the air to settle airway inflammation
options.E: It keeps the small airways splinted open so less air is trapped

correct_answer: E. It keeps the small airways splinted open so less air is trapped
why_correct: In emphysema the small airways collapse early on breathing out because the lung has lost its elastic recoil. Breathing out against pursed lips creates back-pressure that holds these airways open for longer, so air is trapped less and the breathing cycle becomes slower and more efficient. This reduces dynamic hyperinflation and the sensation of breathlessness. Source: standard respiratory physiotherapy teaching for COPD (British Lung Foundation and NHS patient advice); NICE NG115 (2018) recommends pulmonary rehabilitation and breathlessness self-management.
why_wrong: A. The technique slows the breathing rate rather than raising it, so minute ventilation is not increased. B. Patients with advanced COPD are often already retaining carbon dioxide, and the aim is never to raise it. C. A slow, controlled expiration is used here; sputum clearance needs different techniques such as the active cycle of breathing. D. The nose, not the pursed lips, warms the inspired air, and the technique does not treat inflammation.
pearl: Pursed-lip breathing is a free, quick self-management skill that patients can use during exertion or an episode of breathlessness.
thinking: Emphysema with early airway collapse  ↓  Breathing out through pursed lips adds back-pressure  ↓  Airways stay open and less air is trapped  ↓  Breathlessness eases
exam_trap: Do not choose a speed-up or carbon dioxide answer; the technique slows breathing and works by mechanical splinting of the airways.
takeaway: Pursed-lip breathing keeps collapsible airways open during expiration, reducing air trapping and breathlessness in COPD.
notes: Source key and options sound; the AKT stem was a one-liner, rebuilt as a physiotherapy vignette with a new distractor set. No live PLAB 1 item tests pursed-lip breathing (searched pursed, breathing technique, expiration, physio). No figures. Technique is standard teaching; the only NICE page fetched was NG115, which supports pulmonary rehabilitation but does not describe the technique itself.

stem:
A 74-year-old man has had three weeks of slowly worsening breathlessness on exertion. He has no fever and no chest pain. The left side of his chest expands less than the right. There is a stony-dull percussion note over the left base, and breath sounds there are very quiet.

Which investigation should be requested first?
why_correct: Reduced expansion, a stony-dull percussion note and diminished breath sounds at one base indicate a pleural effusion. A chest X-ray is the first-line, widely available test to confirm fluid; it is followed by thoracic ultrasound to guide sampling and then diagnostic pleural aspiration if the cause is unclear. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023 (standard teaching; page not fetched).
why_wrong: B. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and would not explain focal dullness. C. Bronchoscopy is an invasive test reserved for later, once imaging and pleural sampling have guided the diagnosis. D. A CT pulmonary angiogram is for suspected pulmonary embolism, which does not fit a three-week gradual history with focal dullness. E. Echocardiography may be useful later for a cardiac cause but does not confirm the effusion.
pearl: Stony dullness with absent breath sounds at a base is an effusion until proved otherwise, and the chest X-ray comes before ultrasound, aspiration or bronchoscopy.
thinking: Slow breathlessness with unilateral basal dullness  ↓  Think pleural effusion  ↓  Confirm with simple imaging first  ↓  Chest X-ray, then ultrasound-guided sampling
exam_trap: Do not jump to an invasive or specialised test; a plain chest X-ray is the starting point.
takeaway: Suspected pleural effusion is confirmed first with a chest X-ray.
notes: Source key sound. Live BX266 tests the diagnosis from bilateral dullness in heart failure and CR062/RES018/RES031 test fluid analysis; none tests first investigation for suspected effusion. New vignette (man, gradual course, reduced expansion and stony dullness) with different options. BTS 2023 guideline cited as standard teaching only (not fetched).

presentation: Chronic cough and breathlessness in a smoker
stem:
A 62-year-old woman has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for most of her adult life. For two years she has had a productive cough each morning and now becomes breathless climbing a single flight of stairs. She has never been diagnosed with asthma, and her chest examination is unremarkable apart from a prolonged expiratory phase.

Which test is needed to confirm the diagnosis you suspect?

options.D: High-resolution CT scan of the chest

why_correct: A long smoking history with chronic cough and exertional breathlessness suggests chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Diagnosis rests on spirometry performed after a bronchodilator showing persistent airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7), alongside the clinical picture. Source: NICE NG115 (2018, recommendation 1.1.5, checked on the fetched page).
why_wrong: A. An ECG assesses rhythm and ischaemia and does not demonstrate airflow obstruction. B. A peak flow diary looks for variable obstruction and supports asthma rather than confirming COPD. C. Sputum culture helps to guide treatment of an infective exacerbation but does not diagnose COPD. D. High-resolution CT is used to characterise suspected interstitial or structural lung disease and is not required to confirm COPD.
pearl: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude COPD, and a CT scan is not the diagnostic test.
thinking: Heavy smoker, chronic cough, breathless  ↓  Suspect COPD  ↓  Need objective proof of airflow obstruction  ↓  Post-bronchodilator spirometry
exam_trap: Do not pick imaging because the symptoms are respiratory; the diagnosis of COPD is physiological, not radiological.
takeaway: COPD is confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing persistent airflow obstruction.
notes: Source key sound. Live PAQ15631 gives spirometry in the stem and asks for the diagnosis, and GF046/GF048 test interpretation or treatment; none asks which test confirms COPD. Figure retained only as the standard 0.7 ratio (NG115), a long-standing cut-off and not the answer itself. New vignette (woman, 25/day, stairs).

stem:
A 68-year-old man who stopped smoking a few years ago has had a persistent cough and weight loss for three months. A chest X-ray shows a mass at the left hilum, and he has been referred on the suspected cancer pathway (an urgent, time-limited route to specialist assessment). His GP also notes that one area of his chest wheezes, and the sound does not change after he coughs or uses salbutamol.

Which finding is most directly explained by the tumour narrowing the left main bronchus?

options.A: Painful swelling of the wrists and ankles alongside finger clubbing
options.B: Fine crackles heard at both lung bases at the end of inspiration
options.C: Swelling of both ankles together with a raised jugular venous pressure
options.D: A wheeze in one part of the chest that persists after coughing
options.E: Sharp pain in the side of the chest on deep inspiration

correct_answer: D. A wheeze in one part of the chest that persists after coughing
why_correct: A tumour growing in or pressing on a main bronchus narrows the lumen, so air moving through the narrowed segment makes a localised wheeze that persists and does not clear with coughing or bronchodilators. A fixed, unilateral wheeze in a smoker or ex-smoker should prompt imaging for lung cancer rather than a trial of asthma treatment. Source: NICE NG12 (suspected cancer, lung cancer recommendations 1.1.1-1.1.3) and standard respiratory teaching.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is a paraneoplastic effect, not a result of airway obstruction. B. Bilateral basal end-inspiratory crackles point to interstitial fibrosis or left heart failure, not a single obstructing lesion. C. Ankle swelling with a raised venous pressure suggests right heart failure, which is not caused by a unilateral bronchial tumour. E. Pleuritic pain reflects pleural involvement, whereas obstruction of a bronchus causes airway noise or collapse.
pearl: A localised wheeze that persists after coughing suggests a fixed obstruction, unlike the variable, widespread wheeze of asthma.
thinking: Hilar mass on chest X-ray  ↓  Tumour narrows main bronchus  ↓  Air through narrowed segment  ↓  Persistent localised wheeze
exam_trap: A paraneoplastic sign such as clubbing or joint pain is not caused by airway obstruction, so do not pick it for a mechanical question.
takeaway: Narrowing of a main bronchus by a central tumour causes a persistent, localised wheeze.
notes: Source learning point sound and not repeated: live PAQ15774, RES019, RES037 and PAAKT019 test SIADH, Pancoast and CT staging, not local bronchial obstruction (searched wheeze with cancer, central mass, lobar collapse). Vignette, options and framing rewritten with ex-smoker, suspected cancer pathway explained in-stem. Wording of NG12 recommendations checked on the fetched page.
